claim: During M phase, Endosulfine (Endos) family proteins are phosphorylated by Greatwall kinase (Gwl).
source: During M phase, Endosulfine (Endos) family proteins are phosphorylated by Greatwall kinase (Gwl), and the resultant pEndos inhibits the phosphatase PP2A-B55, which would otherwise prematurely reverse many CDK-driven phosphorylations.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by citations to prior work (Gharbi-Ayachi et al., 2010; Mochida et al., 2010) mentioned later in the introduction.

claim: Gwl-phosphorylated Endos (pEndos) inhibits the phosphatase PP2A-B55.
source: During M phase, Endosulfine (Endos) family proteins are phosphorylated by Greatwall kinase (Gwl), and the resultant pEndos inhibits the phosphatase PP2A-B55, which would otherwise prematurely reverse many CDK-driven phosphorylations.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations (Gharbi-Ayachi et al., 2010; Mochida et al., 2010) and is a central finding of the manuscript.

claim: PP2A-B55 is the enzyme responsible for dephosphorylating pEndos during M phase exit.
source: We show here that PP2A-B55 is the enzyme responsible for dephosphorylating pEndos during M phase exit.
evidence: This is the main finding of the manuscript, supported by multiple experimental approaches including RNAi depletion, mutant analysis, and biochemical purification.

claim: The kcat for PP2A-B55's dephosphorylation of pEndos is two to three orders of magnitude slower than for CDK-phosphorylated substrates.
source: The kinetic parameters for PP2A-B55's action on pEndos are orders of magnitude lower than those for CDK-phosphorylated substrates
evidence: This is directly measured in the kinetic experiments presented in Table 1 and Figure 7.

claim: The Km for PP2A-B55's dephosphorylation of pEndos is four to five orders of magnitude lower than for CDK-phosphorylated substrates.
source: the Km values for the two substrates differ by more than four and perhaps even five orders of magnitude
evidence: This is directly measured in the kinetic experiments presented in Table 1 and Figure 7.

claim: Entry of cells into M phase requires the phosphorylation of thousands of sites on hundreds of proteins.
source: Entry of cells into M phase of mitosis or meiosis requires the phosphorylation of thousands of sites on hundreds of proteins (Dephoure et al., 2008; Lindqvist et al., 2009; Dulla et al., 2010; Olsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior phosphoproteomics studies.

claim: Many M phase-specific phosphorylations are substrates of cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs).
source: Many of these sites are substrates of cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), most notably MPF (M phase-promoting factor; CDK1-Cyclin B).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations (Nigg, 1993; Holmes and Solomon, 1996).

claim: PP2A-B55 is the phosphatase responsible for removing many key CDK-generated phosphorylations at the conclusion of M phase.
source: PP2A-B55 (heterotrimeric protein phosphatase 2A composed of a catalytic C subunit, a structural A subunit, and a B55-type regulatory subunit) is the phosphatase responsible for removing many key CDK-generated phosphorylations at the conclusion of M phase (Clarke et al., 1993; Mayer-Jaekel et al., 1994; Mochida and Hunt, 2007; Castilho et al., 2009; Mochida et al., 2009; Schmitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: PP2A-B55 activity must be downregulated when cells go into M phase.
source: The circuitry's basic logic suggests that PP2A-B55 activity must be downregulated when cells go into M phase; if not, the phosphorylations catalyzed by MPF would be prematurely removed, preventing M phase entry (Clarke et al., 1993; Lee et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a logical inference supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MPF phosphorylates and thereby activates the Greatwall kinase (Gwl).
source: In brief, MPF phosphorylates and thereby activates the Greatwall kinase (Gwl) (Yu et al., 2006; Blake-Hodek et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Activated Gwl phosphorylates small proteins of the Endosulfine family at a unique, highly conserved site.
source: Activated Gwl phosphorylates small proteins of the Endosulfine family (Endos; [Gharbi-Ayachi et al., 2010; Mochida et al., 2010]) at a unique, highly conserved site.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The Gwl→pEndos ⊣ PP2A-B55 pathway is critical for M phase entry and maintenance in frog egg extracts, starfish oocytes, and in many cell types in culture or within metazoan organisms.
source: The Gwl→pEndos ⊣ PP2A-B55 pathway is critical for M phase entry and maintenance in frog egg extracts, starfish oocytes, and in many cell types in culture or within metazoan organisms (Archambault et al., 2007; Burgess et al., 2010; Hara et al., 2012; Lorca et al., 2010; Voets and Wolthuis, 2010; Yu et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Considerable anti-Endos activity is present during M phase in Xenopus egg extracts.
source: Figure 2A shows that in accordance with this prediction, considerable anti-Endos activity is indeed seen during M phase.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Anti-CDKS activity (PP2A-B55) is completely blocked in M phase extracts and strongly induced by treatment with Ca2+.
source: As expected from previous studies (Mochida and Hunt, 2007; Castilho et al., 2009), anti-CDKS activity (i.e., PP2A-B55) was completely blocked in M phase extracts and strongly induced by treatment with Ca2+ (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 2A and is consistent with prior work.

claim: All anti-Endos activity in extracts is sensitive to okadaic acid and calyculin A.
source: All of the activity in all extracts tested was suppressed by relatively low doses of okadaic acid or calyculin A (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 2B and supplemental figures.

claim: Anti-Endos activity is completely resistant to the calcineurin (PP2B) inhibitor cyclosporin A.
source: but was completely resistant to the calcineurin (PP2B) inhibitor cyclosporin A (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result, though the data is not shown.

claim: The enzyme(s) targeting the Gwl site in Endos belong to the PPP family of phospho-serine/threonine protein phosphatases.
source: These results indicate that the enzyme(s) targeting the Gwl site in Endos belong to the PPP family of phospho-serine/threonine protein phosphatases, which include PP1, PP2A, PP4, PP5, and PP6 (Swingle et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the inhibitor sensitivity data and supported by citation to prior work on phosphatase classification.

claim: The majority of anti-Endos activity (70-90% of the total) is sensitive to fostriecin and is thus due to PP2A, PP4, or PP6.
source: The predominant anti-Endos activity in many cell types (∼70–90% of the total depending on the experiment) is thus due to PP2A, PP4, or PP6.
evidence: This is inferred from the fostriecin sensitivity data shown in Figure 2C and supplemental figures.

claim: Anti-Endos activity is 6- to 10-fold more resistant to tautomycetin than anti-CDKS activity.
source: In contrast, the anti-Endos activity in all extracts tested is 6- to 10-fold more resistant to tautomycetin than is anti-CDKS (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B–F).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 2D and supplemental figures.

claim: Anti-Endos activity is relatively unaffected by the presence of constitutively activated Endos (S68D phosphomimetic).
source: However, the anti-Endos activity in extracts is substantially resistant to inhibition by phosphomimetic Drosophila Endos (S68D) (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 2E and supplemental figures.

claim: Dilution of cellular extracts leads to large increases in the specific activity of anti-CDKS and anti-H1v1.0, but anti-Endos activity is much less affected by extract dilution.
source: We have verified this dilution effect for anti-CDKS and anti-H1v1.0, but in contrast, anti-Endos activity is very much less affected by extract dilution (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 2F and supplemental figures.

claim: Treatment of Drosophila S2 cells with dsRNAs for the PP2A catalytic subunit gene (mts) caused the loss of 70-75% of the anti-Endos activity.
source: Treatment of Drosophila S2 cells with dsRNAs for the single PP2A catalytic subunit gene in the fly genome (called mts) caused the loss of 70–75% of the anti-Endos activity (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Depletion of the A (structural) subunit of PP2A caused substantial loss of anti-Endos activity.
source: Depletion of the A (structural) subunit of PP2A also caused substantial loss of anti-Endos activity (Figure 3)
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: RNAi for PP1-87B only slightly decreased anti-Endos activity.
source: In contrast, RNAi for PP1-87B, whose product accounts for more than 80% of the PP1 activity in Drosophila larvae (Dombradi et al., 1990), only slightly decreased anti-Endos (Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: dsRNAs against coding sequences for PP4, PP5, and PP6 catalytic subunits had no obvious effects on anti-Endos levels.
source: dsRNAs against coding sequences for all other PPP family catalytic subunits (PP4, PP5, and PP6) had no obvious effects on anti-Endos levels (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result, though the data is not shown.

claim: Treatment of HeLa cells with siRNA to the PP4 catalytic subunit does not affect anti-Endos levels.
source: Treatment of HeLa cells with siRNA to the PP4 catalytic subunit strongly reduces the amount of PP4 but does not obviously affect anti-Endos levels.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Mouse MEF cells homozygous for a knockout allele of the PP5 gene display the same levels of anti-Endos and anti-CDKS activities as control cells.
source: Mouse MEF cells homozygous for a knockout allele of the PP5 gene (Yong et al., 2007) also displayed the same levels of anti-Endos and anti-CDKS activities as control cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Drosophila larvae homozygous for mutations in twins (the gene encoding the sole B55-type subunit in flies) lack both anti-CDKS and anti-Endos activities.
source: Relative to wild-type, larvae homozygous for mutations in twins (the gene encoding the sole B55-type subunit in flies) were not only deficient in anti-CDKS as expected, but they also lacked anti-Endos; the same was true for brains isolated from these larvae (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Activities against Histone H1v1.0 were virtually unaffected in twins mutant larvae.
source: Activities against Histone H1v1.0 were virtually unaffected in twins mutants.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Twins mutant larvae had no detectable Twins (B55) protein on Western blots.
source: On Western blots, the twins larvae had no detectable Twins (B55) protein
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Gross levels of PP2A-A and PP2A-C were not diminished by the absence of Twins in twins mutant larvae.
source: moreover, gross levels of PP2A-A and PP2A-C were not diminished by the absence of Twins (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the Western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: None of the phosphatase activities (anti-Endos, anti-CDKS, anti-Histone H1v1.0) were altered in larvae carrying mutations in genes for any other tested PP2A regulatory subunit, for the PPP4R3 regulatory subunit of PP4 (flfl), or for any of the PP1 catalytic subunits (with the possible exception of a decrease in Histone H1v1.0 dephosphorylation in PP1-87B larvae).
source: None of these phosphatase activities were altered in larvae carrying mutations in genes for any other tested PP2A regulatory subunit, for the PPP4R3 regulatory subunit of PP4 (flfl), or for any of the PP1 catalytic subunits (with the possible exception of a decrease in Histone H1v1.0 dephosphorylation in PP1-87B larvae; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Anti-Endos and anti-CDKS activities co-purified during Mono-Q chromatography of HeLa cell extracts.
source: Assays of the fractions revealed that anti-Endos and anti-CDKS activities co-purified.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the fractionation data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The peak activities of anti-Endos and anti-CDKS coincided with the fractions containing the three components of PP2A-B55 (the A, B55, and C subunits).
source: The peak activities towards both substrates coincided with the fractions containing the three components of PP2A-B55 (the A, B55, and C subunits), although the PP1 catalytic subunit was also found in these same fractions.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the fractionation and Western blot data shown in Figure 5.

claim: PP5 and PP6 elute from the Mono-Q column at much lower salt concentrations than the peak anti-Endos/anti-CDKS fractions.
source: PP5 and PP6 elute from the Mono-Q column at much lower salt concentrations, while PP4 and the B56 and B‴ (striatin) regulatory subunits of PP2A elute at higher salt than the peak anti-Endos/anti-CDKS (Figure 5).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the fractionation and Western blot data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Purified recombinant PP2A-B55 heterotrimers containing B55α and B55δ isoforms efficiently dephosphorylated pEndos and pCDKS substrates.
source: Heterotrimers containing B55α and B55δ isoforms efficiently dephosphorylated pEndos and pCDKS substrates (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Control PP2A-B56β heterotrimers and empty vector preparations displayed no activity against pEndos or pCDKS substrates.
source: Neither control PP2A-B56β heterotrimers nor empty vector preparations made in parallel displayed any activity against either substrate.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Purified PP2A-A/C dimers do not target pEndos or pCDKS substrates even when in 10-fold excess relative to the heterotrimeric holoenzymes.
source: Neither the anti-Endos nor anti-CDKS functions of the PP2A-B55 preparations could be attributed to heterotrimer dissociation into A–C dimers, because purified dimer does not target either substrate even when in 10-fold excess relative to the heterotrimeric holoenzymes (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The anti-Endos and anti-CDKS activities of purified PP2A-B55 heterotrimer were similarly sensitive to fostriecin.
source: The anti-Endos and anti-CDKS activities of the PP2A-B55 heterotrimer were similarly sensitive to fostriecin, as expected if the catalytic subunit is the same (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The anti-Endos activity of purified PP2A-B55 was much less sensitive to either tautomycetin or phosphomimetic Endos than was the anti-CDKS activity of the same preparations.
source: However, the anti-Endos activity of PP2A-B55 was much less sensitive to either tautomycetin or phosphomimetic Endos than was the anti-CDKS activity of the same preparations (Figure 6C,D)
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: pEndos does not inhibit its own dephosphorylation by PP2A-B55 at high substrate concentrations.
source: Such allosteric down-regulation would cause the rate of pEndos dephosphorylation to decrease when the substrate is added at very high concentrations, but this is not the case (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 7B, where the rate remains constant over a 20-fold range of pEndos concentration.

claim: pEndos competes with okadaic acid for binding to PP2A-B55.
source: pEndos competes with okadaic acid, a drug known to bind only to PP2A's active site (Xing et al., 2006).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the okadaic acid competition experiments shown in Figure 7D,E and is supported by citation to prior work on okadaic acid binding.

claim: The IC50 of thiophosphorylated Endos for inhibiting PP2A-B55 is 197 ± 14 pM.
source: The IC50 of thiophosphorylated Endos determined in this way was 197 ± 14 pM
evidence: This is directly measured in the inhibition experiments shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The IC50 of nonphosphorylated Endos for inhibiting PP2A-B55 is 566 ± 65 nM.
source: by comparison, the IC50 of nonphosphorylated Endos was measured to be 566 ± 65 nM.
evidence: This is directly measured in the inhibition experiments shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Thiophosphorylation of Endos increases its binding affinity for PP2A-B55 about 3000-fold compared to nonphosphorylated Endos.
source: Thus, the (thio)phosphorylation of Endos increases its binding affinity for PP2A-B55 about 3000-fold.
evidence: This is calculated from the IC50 values measured in the inhibition experiments shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The IC50 of thiophosphorylated Endos is only about twice that of okadaic acid for inhibiting PP2A-B55.
source: Indicative of the strong affinity between activated Endos and PP2A-B55, the IC50 of thiophosphorylated Endos is only about twice that of okadaic acid measured in similar assays (107 ± 10 pM Figure 8A)
evidence: This is directly measured in the inhibition experiments shown in Figure 8A.

claim: PP2A-B55 can auto-reactivate by dephosphorylating pEndos inhibitor that can no longer be replenished once Gwl is inactivated.
source: One prediction of the inhibition by unfair competition hypothesis is that PP2A-B55 should be able to auto-reactivate at the conclusion of M phase. By dephosphorylating pEndos inhibitor that can no longer be replenished once Gwl is inactivated, PP2A-B55 is now freed to recognize its normal, CDK-phosphorylated substrates.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 8B, where PP2A-B55 activity against pCDKS is restored after pEndos is depleted.

claim: PP2A-B55 cannot recognize pCDKS substrate until the majority of pEndos in the same reaction has been dephosphorylated.
source: Comparing the effects of pEndos inhibition after 30- and 120-min incubations demonstrates that PP2A-B55 cannot recognize the pCDKS substrate until the majority of the pEndos in the same tube has been dephosphorylated.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: A clear delay in pCDKS dephosphorylation of roughly 35 min is visible in samples containing pEndos, after which the rate of the reaction approaches the initial rate observed in the absence of Endos inhibitors.
source: A clear delay in pCDKS dephosphorylation of roughly 35 min is visible in the sample containing pEndos, after which the rate of the reaction approaches the initial rate observed in the absence of Endos inhibitors.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The intracellular concentration of the PP2A B55 subunit is estimated to be between 100 and 250 nM.
source: From our own quantitation on Western blots, we estimate the intracellular concentration of the PP2A B55 subunit to be between 100 and 250 nM
evidence: This is estimated from Western blot quantitation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The intracellular concentration of Endos is estimated to be between 500 nM and 1 μM.
source: and that of Endos to be between 500 nM and 1 μΜ, depending on the cell type.
evidence: This is estimated from Western blot quantitation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: The 5:1 ratio of Endos to PP2A-B55 is roughly consistent with estimates from other laboratories and from mass spectrometry studies.
source: The 5:1 ratio of Endos to PP2A-B55 observed in that figure is roughly consistent with estimates from other laboratories (Cundell et al., 2013) and with estimates from mass spectrometry studies of whole cell extracts, after accounting for all Endos and PP2A-B55 family members (Brunner et al., 2007; Beck et al., 2011; Kolker et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and mass spectrometry data.

claim: The proportion of total Endos protein that is phosphorylated during M phase is roughly 50% in extracts of synchronized mammalian tissue culture cells.
source: Although we ourselves have not determined the fraction of the total Endos protein that is phosphorylated during M phase, other investigators have found that this proportion is roughly 50% in extracts of synchronized mammalian tissue culture cells (perhaps some of which may not have been in M phase) (Cundell et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The proportion of total Endos protein that is phosphorylated during M phase approaches 100% in frog egg M phase extracts.
source: and approaches 100% in frog egg M phase extracts (Mochida et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Half of PP2A-B55 is released from pEndos sequestration within 74 seconds after Gwl inactivation at the end of M phase, according to theoretical modeling.
source: Beyond this point, PP2A-B55 is rapidly released from sequestration; half is available to act on other substrates within 74 s (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is calculated from the theoretical model shown in Figure 10A using physiological parameters.

claim: If pEndos were only an inhibitor and not a substrate of PP2A-B55, many hours would be required for PP2A-B55 desequestration and M phase exit.
source: In this scenario, PP2A-B55 would protect the bound pEndos from dephosphorylation, so many hours—not just a few minutes—would be required for PP2A-B55 desequestration and M phase exit.
evidence: This is calculated from the theoretical model shown in Figure 10C,D.

claim: The dephosphorylation of pEndos by PP2A-B55 is an absolute requirement for rapid completion of the M phase-to-interphase transition.
source: In other words, the dephosphorylation of pEndos by PP2A-B55 is an absolute requirement for rapid completion of the M phase-to-interphase transition.
evidence: This is inferred from the theoretical modeling shown in Figure 10.

claim: Depletion of more than 90% of Fcp1 in Drosophila S2 cells has no obvious effect on the ability of extracts to dephosphorylate pEndos.
source: RNAi depletion of more than 90% of the Fcp1 in Drosophila S2 cells has no obvious effect on the ability of extracts made from these cells to dephosphorylate pEndos (Figure 11A,B).
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 11A,B.

claim: Purified S. pombe Fcp1 enzyme has detectable anti-Endos activity, but this is very low.
source: Purified S. pombe Fcp1 enzyme has detectable anti-Endos activity, but this is very low.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 11C,D.

claim: At a physiological concentration of pEndos (1 μM), each molecule of Fcp1 has less than 1/1,000th the efficiency of a molecule of PP2A-B55 in dephosphorylating this substrate.
source: At a physiological concentration of the pEndos (1 μM), each molecule of Fcp1 has less than 1/1,000th the efficiency of a molecule of PP2A-B55 in dephosphorylating this substrate (Figure 11C,D).
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data shown in Figure 11C,D.

claim: Cells contain more than 10 times more PP2A-B55 than Fcp1 molecules.
source: Moreover, cells contain more than 10 times more PP2A-B55 than Fcp1 molecules (based on values in the Pax-DB database of protein abundances determined by mass spectrometry; see www.pax-db.org and reference Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to mass spectrometry database.

claim: Less than 0.01% of the total anti-Endos activity in cells can be ascribed to Fcp1.
source: By this estimate, less than 0.01% of the total anti-Endos activity in cells can be ascribed to Fcp1.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data and protein abundance estimates.

claim: Fcp1 is completely resistant to okadaic acid.
source: yet the literature contains many reports that Fcp1 is completely resistant to okadaic acid (e.g., Palancade et al., 2001; Washington et al., 2002; Kong et al., 2005; Visconti et al., 2012), a fact that we verify in our Figure 11E.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the experimental data shown in Figure 11E and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In mono-Q chromatography, Fcp1 does not co-fractionate with the pEndos-dephosphorylating activity.
source: In mono-Q chromatography, Fcp1 does not co-fractionate with the pEndos-dephosphorylating activity. Figure 5 shows that fractions with peak anti-Endos activity (such as fractions from 37 to 39) have no detectable Fcp1 protein.
evidence: This is directly demonstrated by the fractionation and Western blot data shown in Figure 5.

claim: An inhibitor will be effective only if its Ki is less than the Km for the substrate.
source: In each case, the discrepancy is explained by careful quantitative attention to the relationship between the Ki of the inhibitor and the Km of the target: roughly speaking, an inhibitor will be effective only if its Ki is less than the Km for the substrate.
evidence: This is a general principle of enzyme kinetics applied to explain the data.

claim: Tautomycetin has an IC50 of 62 nM for PP2A.
source: Thus, as was seen in Figure 6C, tautomycetin, which has an IC50 (which provides a very rough estimate of Ki) of 62 nM (Mitsuhashi et al., 2001)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The IC50 of Drosophila S68D Endos phosphomimetic protein is approximately 500 nM.
source: The same consideration explains the difference in inhibition by the Drosophila S68 Endos phosphomimetic protein, whose IC50 (approximately 500 nM from Figure 6D)
evidence: This is estimated from the experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: M phase exit is completed within less than 5 minutes in Xenopus cycling extracts.
source: M phase exit is surprisingly rapid given the large number of phosphorylations which must be reversed; in Xenopus cycling extracts, for example, the M phase-to-interphase transition is completed within less than 5 min (Zhao et al., 2008; Mochida et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Endos is present in cells in at most a fivefold stoichiometric excess with respect to PP2A-B55.
source: The reason is that Endos is present in cells only in at most a fivefold stoichiometric excess with respect to the phosphatase, as was just discussed.
evidence: This is estimated from Western blot quantitation and mass spectrometry data discussed earlier.

claim: PKA-phosphorylated Inhibitor-1 acts both as an inhibitor and a substrate for PP1.
source: In short, just as we report here for pEndos and PP2A-B55, they concluded that pInhibitor-1 acts both as an inhibitor and a substrate for PP1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Foulkes et al., 1983).

claim: The values of Km and kcat for PP1 dephosphorylation of PKA-phosphorylated Inhibitor-1 were both considerably lower than for dephosphorylation of the more normal substrate phosphorylase a.
source: The investigators found that purified PP1 could dephosphorylate PKA-phosphorylated Inhibitor-1, and the values of Km and kcat were both considerably lower for this reaction than for dephosphorylation of the more normal substrate phosphorylase a (Foulkes et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: PP1's activity in inactivating pInhibitor-1 was very slow.
source: These observations have long since been disregarded because PP1's activity in inactivating pInhibitor-1 was very slow
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Ingebritsen et al., 1983; Cohen, 1989).

claim: Other phosphatases (PP2A and calcineurin) had substantial pInhibitor-1 dephosphorylating activity.
source: and other phosphatases (PP2A and calcineurin) had substantial pInhibitor-1 dephosphorylating activity (Ingebritsen et al., 1983; Cohen, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Recent studies in Xenopus egg extracts have indicated that pInhibitor-1 dephosphorylation at the end of M phase is dependent upon activity of PP1.
source: Of interest, recent studies in Xenopus egg extracts have indicated that pInhibitor-1 dephosphorylation at the end of M phase is in fact dependent upon activity of PP1, although this work could not distinguish whether the effect was direct or indirect (Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.
